subtopic_detail: Gender affirming care pathway in a young adult
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 19 year old man in an outpatient clinic. He was assigned female at birth, has lived and worked in his affirmed gender for three years, and has used his current name on all documents for two of those years.

He asks to start testosterone. He had a depressive episode at 16 that has been in full remission on sertraline 50 mg daily for two years. He describes a consistent and long standing sense of his gender, has a supportive partner and household, and reports no suicidal ideation. He has never had gender affirming hormone therapy and takes no other medication.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychotic features, capacity to consent intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function, renal function and lipids within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Require a further 12 months of psychotherapy before considering any referral onward
options.rationale: A mandatory psychotherapy period is not a current requirement and functions as a gatekeeping barrier that delays care without improving outcomes (Source: AusPATH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse People).
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse People

options.text: Refer him for gender affirming hormone therapy assessment and continue his sertraline
options.rationale: A consistent long standing gender identity with intact capacity and a stably remitted mood disorder supports referral for hormone therapy assessment now, with existing mental health treatment continued alongside rather than as a precondition (Source: AusPATH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse People).
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse People

options.text: Cease his sertraline first so that his baseline mood state can be properly established
options.rationale: Withdrawing effective maintenance treatment risks relapse of a depressive illness and creates a fresh barrier, since remission on treatment is not a diagnostic obstacle (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Advise a documented period of real life experience before any medical treatment starts
options.rationale: A formally imposed real life experience requirement has been removed from current standards, and in any case he has already lived in his affirmed gender for three years (Source: AusPATH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse People).
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse People

options.text: Defer any decision until he turns 21 given the permanence of some hormonal effects
options.rationale: He is an adult with capacity, so an arbitrary age threshold has no clinical or legal basis and simply postpones an assessment he is already eligible for (Source: AusPATH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse People).
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse People

explanation.summary: Australian standards have moved from a gatekeeping model to an informed consent model, in which the psychiatrist's role is to assess capacity, confirm a consistent gender identity and treat any co-occurring mental illness rather than to authorise treatment. Co-occurring depression and anxiety are common in trans and gender diverse populations and are strongly associated with minority stress and delayed care, so treating them is complementary to affirming care rather than a barrier to it. Mental illness in remission does not preclude referral, and only conditions that actively impair capacity to consent are relevant obstacles. Delay carries its own measurable harm, with elevated rates of self harm and suicide attempt reported while people wait for access.
key_points: Australian practice follows an informed consent model rather than a gatekeeping model
The psychiatrist assesses capacity and consistency of identity, not eligibility for treatment
Remitted or treated mental illness is not a barrier to referral
A mandated real life experience period is no longer part of current standards
explanation.pearls: Testosterone induced voice deepening and clitoral growth are irreversible while fat redistribution and menstrual suppression are not, so the consent discussion separates these two groups of effects explicitly rather than treating hormone therapy as a single reversible decision.

sources.label: AusPATH Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse People
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Advance statements and supported decision making
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 38 year old woman who has recovered from her third episode of psychosis and is being prepared for discharge. She has capacity today and is working with her case manager on relapse prevention.

She tells you that during her last admission she was given haloperidol, which caused a severe dystonic reaction she found frightening, and that she responded well to olanzapine on both other occasions. She wants this recorded so that it is followed if she becomes unwell again and cannot speak for herself. She also wants her brother, rather than her father, to be the person clinicians contact and involve in decisions during any future admission.

data_table.Examination: No psychotic symptoms elicited, insight good, capacity intact on formal assessment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to give effect to her wishes?

options.text: Record her preferences as a clinical file note for the treating team to consider
options.rationale: A file note has no standing under mental health legislation and is easily overlooked at a future presentation, so it does not achieve what she is asking for (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 guidance; RANZCP Code of Ethics).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 guidance

options.text: Apply to the tribunal for a treatment order specifying olanzapine as the sole agent
options.rationale: Compulsory treatment orders are for patients who meet criteria for involuntary treatment, and applying for one for a well patient with capacity is neither lawful nor necessary (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 guidance).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 guidance

options.text: Ask her general practitioner to add an allergy alert for haloperidol to her records
options.rationale: An alert captures the adverse drug reaction but carries none of her positive treatment preference and does nothing about who should be involved in her care (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).

options.text: Support her to make an advance statement and formally nominate her support person
options.rationale: Australian mental health legislation provides for advance statements of preference and for a nominated support person, and both mechanisms are made while the person has capacity so that clinicians must have regard to them during a later episode (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 guidance).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 guidance

options.text: Advise that her stated preferences cannot bind a future team and reassure her instead
options.rationale: This confuses the fact that an advance statement can be departed from with the false claim that it has no force, when clinicians must consider it and record written reasons for any departure (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 guidance).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 guidance

explanation.summary: Advance statements of preference and nominated support persons are the two main supported decision making instruments in contemporary Australian mental health legislation, and the detail varies between states and territories while the principle does not. They are made while the person has capacity and record what treatment they would want, what they would refuse, and who should be involved. A treating clinician is not absolutely bound but must have regard to the statement and, in most jurisdictions, give written reasons when departing from it. Made well, they reduce the use of restrictive interventions and improve the therapeutic relationship, and the point of maximal recovery just before discharge is the ideal moment to write one.
key_points: Advance statements are made while the person has capacity and record treatment preferences
A nominated support person is a separate formal appointment from next of kin
Clinicians must have regard to an advance statement and document reasons for departing from it
The instruments differ in name and detail across states and territories
explanation.pearls: Write the advance statement in the days before discharge rather than at the next admission, because capacity is at its clearest then and the specific adverse reaction the patient wants avoided is still fresh enough to be described precisely.

sources.label: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 guidance

subtopic_detail: Culturally safe engagement and social and emotional wellbeing
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar at a regional hospital. A 22 year old Aboriginal man is referred by the emergency department after presenting with three months of low mood, poor sleep and heavy alcohol use following the death of an uncle.

He attended one appointment at the clinic last year and did not return. Today he sits at the edge of the room, gives brief answers and twice says he wants to leave. He denies current suicidal intent and is not intoxicated. He mentions that most of his family live four hours away and that he has been staying with different cousins since the funeral.

data_table.Examination: Guarded, minimal eye contact, no psychotic features, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function, thyroid function and blood alcohol within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate approach to this consultation?

options.text: Offer to involve an Aboriginal health worker and ask who he wants present today
options.rationale: Engagement is the rate limiting step after a previous non return, and offering an Aboriginal health worker together with the patient's own choice of who is present directly addresses cultural safety and the social and emotional wellbeing framework (Source: Gayaa Dhuwi Declaration; National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Plan).
source_refs: National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Plan

options.text: Complete a full structured psychiatric history today before he leaves the department
options.rationale: Pressing a disengaging patient through a long structured interview is the most reliable way to lose him a second time, and the information gained is unlikely to be accurate (Source: Gayaa Dhuwi Declaration).

options.text: Commence an antidepressant now and arrange telephone review again in four weeks
options.rationale: Prescribing before any therapeutic relationship exists and while heavy alcohol use is undressed produces poor adherence, and telephone follow up repeats the pattern that already failed (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Detain him under the mental health act until a full risk assessment can be finished
options.rationale: He denies suicidal intent, is not intoxicated and shows no psychosis, so no legal criterion for detention is met and using the act here would destroy any future engagement (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).

options.text: Refer him to a drug and alcohol service alone and defer mental health review entirely
options.rationale: Splitting grief, depression and alcohol use across separate services creates another referral he can fall through, and the conditions here are plainly interlinked (Source: National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Plan).
source_refs: National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Plan

explanation.summary: The social and emotional wellbeing framework understands mental health as inseparable from connection to family, community, culture, Country and spirituality, and grief and loss sit at its centre rather than at its edge. A previous non attendance is best read as a service level failure of cultural safety rather than as patient level non compliance. Aboriginal health workers and liaison officers are core clinical colleagues in this setting, and their involvement measurably improves engagement and follow up. Practical steps matter as much as principles: asking who the person wants present, allowing more than one shorter contact rather than one long interview, and not forcing a full history at the first meeting.
key_points: Social and emotional wellbeing extends beyond symptoms to family, community, culture and Country
Grief and loss are a central rather than peripheral part of the framework
Aboriginal health workers are clinical colleagues whose involvement improves engagement
Previous non attendance signals a cultural safety problem in the service, not patient failure
explanation.pearls: Offer several short contacts rather than one long structured assessment when a patient has already disengaged once, because completing the paperwork at the first visit routinely costs the second visit entirely.

sources.label: National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Plan
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old woman who has taken risperidone 4 mg daily for eight months for a psychotic illness that is now in full remission. She is adherent and wants to stay well.

She reports that her periods stopped five months ago and that both breasts leak a small amount of milky fluid when pressed. She has never been pregnant and a pregnancy test today is negative. She takes no other medication, has no headache and has no visual field defect on confrontation testing. Her thyroid function is within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Visual fields full to confrontation, no galactorrhoea at rest, no acromegalic features
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1850 mIU/L (less than 500); beta human chorionic gonadotropin not detected; thyroid function and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary before altering her medication
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for prolactin levels out of keeping with the drug, typically above about 4000 mIU/L, or for headache or visual field loss, none of which apply here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Add cabergoline weekly and continue risperidone at her present effective dose
options.rationale: A dopamine agonist directly opposes the mechanism of the antipsychotic and can precipitate relapse of psychosis, so it is a late option rather than a first move (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Switch her to aripiprazole with a cross taper and repeat the prolactin afterwards
options.rationale: Aripiprazole is a partial dopamine agonist and is prolactin sparing, so switching corrects the cause while maintaining antipsychotic cover, and the repeat level confirms resolution (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Prescribe a combined oral contraceptive to restore her menstrual bleeding pattern
options.rationale: This masks the amenorrhoea without lowering prolactin and leaves the galactorrhoea and the underlying oestrogen deficiency untreated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Cease risperidone entirely and monitor her mental state closely over the next month
options.rationale: Stopping antipsychotic cover eight months into remission from a psychotic illness carries a high relapse risk when a prolactin sparing alternative is available (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride cause the highest rates of hyperprolactinaemia among antipsychotics because they block tuberoinfundibular dopamine receptors and lift the tonic inhibition of prolactin release. Symptoms include amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction and, over years, reduced bone mineral density from oestrogen deficiency, which is why the problem is treated rather than tolerated. Drug induced levels usually sit below about 2000 to 3000 mIU/L, and a level substantially above that or any headache or visual field defect should redirect towards pituitary imaging. Aripiprazole is the standard destination because partial dopamine agonism preserves antipsychotic effect while releasing prolactin inhibition.
key_points: Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride carry the highest prolactin liability
Drug induced elevation is usually below about 2000 to 3000 mIU/L
Imaging is triggered by disproportionate levels, headache or visual field defect
Untreated hyperprolactinaemia reduces bone mineral density through oestrogen deficiency
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole added at low dose alongside the existing antipsychotic will also lower prolactin, which is the workaround when a patient has responded only to risperidone and a full switch is judged too risky.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant selection with a cytochrome P450 2D6 interaction
stem:
You are the consultation liaison registrar asked to advise on a 52 year old woman attending the breast clinic. She completed treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer 10 months ago and takes tamoxifen 20 mg daily, which is planned to continue for five years.

Over the past three months she has had persistent low mood, loss of interest, poor concentration and early morning waking, and she scores in the moderate range on a depression rating scale. She has never taken an antidepressant. She has no history of mania, takes no other regular medicines, and her renal function, liver function, sodium and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Investigations: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145); renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate first choice?

options.text: Paroxetine 20 mg daily, increasing to 40 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
options.rationale: Paroxetine is the strongest cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor among the antidepressants and has been associated with increased breast cancer mortality in women taking tamoxifen (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily, increasing to 40 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is also a potent cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor and its long half life means the interaction persists for weeks after any dose change (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily, increasing to 300 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
options.rationale: Bupropion is a moderate to strong cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor and is not registered as an antidepressant in Australia, so it fails on both interaction and availability grounds (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Duloxetine 30 mg daily, increasing to 60 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
options.rationale: Duloxetine is a moderate cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor, so it is a less clean choice than an agent with negligible effect on that enzyme (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Escitalopram 10 mg daily, increasing to 20 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
options.rationale: Escitalopram has negligible cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibition and so does not impair the conversion of tamoxifen to its active metabolite endoxifen, making it the standard first choice in this setting (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; eviQ Cancer Treatments Online).

explanation.summary: Tamoxifen is a prodrug that requires cytochrome P450 2D6 to be converted to endoxifen, the metabolite responsible for most of its antioestrogen activity. Strong inhibitors of that enzyme reduce endoxifen concentrations substantially, and observational data link paroxetine co prescription with increased breast cancer mortality. Depression is common after breast cancer treatment and undertreating it is not the answer, so the task is agent selection rather than avoidance of antidepressants. Escitalopram, citalopram and venlafaxine all have minimal effect on the enzyme, and venlafaxine has the added advantage of evidence for tamoxifen related hot flushes.
key_points: Tamoxifen is a prodrug activated by cytochrome P450 2D6 to endoxifen
Paroxetine and fluoxetine are strong inhibitors and are avoided with tamoxifen
Escitalopram, citalopram and venlafaxine have minimal effect on the enzyme
Depression after breast cancer treatment is treated, not avoided, with careful agent choice
explanation.pearls: Venlafaxine is the preferred choice when the same patient also needs treatment for tamoxifen induced hot flushes, since it spares cytochrome P450 2D6 and reduces flush frequency, whereas paroxetine would treat the flushes while undermining the tamoxifen.

subtopic_detail: Long term benzodiazepine deprescribing in an older patient
stem:
You are the registrar in a general practice clinic seeing a 71 year old woman who has taken temazepam 20 mg nightly for six years, originally prescribed after a bereavement.

She has fallen twice in the past three months, both times when getting up overnight, and sustained a wrist fracture on the second occasion. She says the tablets no longer help her sleep but that she cannot manage without them and becomes anxious if she misses a dose. Her cognition is normal on formal testing, her postural blood pressure drop is 6 mmHg, and her vision, vitamin D and renal function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Gait steady in daylight, no peripheral neuropathy, cognitive screening normal
data_table.Investigations: Renal function, liver function, full blood count and vitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her temazepam?

options.text: Continue temazepam at the current dose and install home rails and night lighting
options.rationale: Environmental modification helps but leaves the single most modifiable falls risk factor in place, and she herself reports the drug no longer produces the intended effect (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Substitute an equivalent diazepam dose and reduce it gradually over several months
options.rationale: Switching to a long acting agent smooths the interdose fall in concentration that drives rebound anxiety, and a slow staged reduction over months is what makes withdrawal tolerable in long term use (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Cease temazepam tonight and prescribe temazepam 10 mg for occasional rescue use
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after six years risks a withdrawal syndrome including seizures, and intermittent rescue dosing perpetuates the dependence it is meant to end (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Replace temazepam with nightly quetiapine 25 mg and review her sleep in one month
options.rationale: Substituting an antipsychotic exchanges one falls risk for another and adds metabolic and extrapyramidal harm, and quetiapine is not indicated for insomnia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Replace temazepam with nightly melatonin and give her written sleep hygiene advice
options.rationale: Melatonin and sleep hygiene are useful adjuncts during a taper but cannot cover an abrupt substitution after six years of physiological dependence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Benzodiazepine use in older people roughly doubles the risk of falls and hip fracture, and tolerance to the hypnotic effect develops within weeks while the falls risk persists indefinitely. Deprescribing is therefore a positive intervention rather than the withdrawal of a comfort, but it fails when it is done abruptly or on a timescale set by the clinician rather than the patient. Substituting a long acting agent such as diazepam is standard when interdose rebound anxiety is prominent, as it is when a short acting hypnotic has been taken nightly for years. Reductions of around 10 to 25 per cent of the dose every one to two weeks, slowing further as the dose falls, are typical, and cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the definitive treatment for the underlying sleep complaint.
key_points: Benzodiazepines roughly double falls and hip fracture risk in older people
Hypnotic tolerance develops within weeks while falls risk does not diminish
Long acting substitution reduces interdose rebound during a taper
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the definitive treatment for the sleep complaint
explanation.pearls: Reduce by about 10 to 25 per cent of the dose every one to two weeks and slow the rate as the total dose falls, because the final 5 mg of diazepam equivalent is reliably harder than the first 20 mg.

stem:
You are the registrar in a perinatal mental health clinic seeing a 30 year old woman who is six weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding a healthy term infant.

She has recurrent major depressive disorder with three previous episodes, one of which required admission. She has taken fluoxetine 20 mg daily for four years, remained on it through pregnancy, and has stayed well throughout including the past six weeks. Her infant is feeding well, is gaining weight along the fiftieth centile and is neurologically normal at the six week check. She asks whether she should stop or change her medication now that she is feeding.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no suicidal ideation, mother and infant interaction warm and responsive
data_table.Investigations: Edinburgh postnatal depression scale score 4; full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her medication?

options.text: Stop fluoxetine now and restart it promptly if any depressive symptoms return
options.rationale: Discontinuation in the first postpartum year in recurrent depression carries a high relapse risk, and waiting for symptoms means intervening after the illness has already returned (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Switch to sertraline because it produces the lowest relative infant dose available
options.rationale: Sertraline is the usual first choice when starting an antidepressant during lactation, but switching an agent that has already kept her well through pregnancy risks relapse for a marginal pharmacokinetic gain (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Halve the dose to 10 mg daily to reduce the total quantity reaching her infant
options.rationale: A subtherapeutic dose exposes the infant to the drug anyway while withdrawing the protection the mother needs, which is the worst of both positions (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Continue fluoxetine unchanged and support her to keep breastfeeding as she wishes
options.rationale: The relative infant dose of fluoxetine sits within the range generally regarded as acceptable, the infant is thriving and neurologically normal, and continuing an agent that has maintained remission through pregnancy is the lowest risk option for both (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Continue fluoxetine and advise her to change to formula feeding to avoid exposure
options.rationale: Ceasing breastfeeding forfeits its established maternal and infant benefits to avoid an exposure that is already within accepted limits in a thriving infant (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Almost all antidepressants pass into breast milk in small quantities, and the relative infant dose, meaning the infant dose expressed as a percentage of the maternal weight adjusted dose, is the standard measure of that exposure. A relative infant dose below 10 per cent is generally regarded as acceptable, and the commonly used antidepressants sit well below that. Sertraline and paroxetine have the lowest relative infant doses and are usual first choices when initiating during lactation, while fluoxetine's longer half life gives it a slightly higher figure that is still within accepted limits. The dominant risk in this scenario is not drug exposure but maternal relapse, which carries measurable harm to infant attachment and development.
key_points: Relative infant dose below 10 per cent is generally regarded as acceptable in lactation
Sertraline has the lowest relative infant dose and is a usual first choice when starting new treatment
An agent already maintaining remission is generally continued rather than switched
Maternal relapse carries its own substantial risk to infant attachment and development
explanation.pearls: Watch a breastfed infant of a mother on fluoxetine for irritability, poor feeding or excess drowsiness rather than for any specific syndrome, since the long half life of norfluoxetine means any effect accumulates over the first weeks rather than appearing immediately.

sources.label: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

subtopic_detail: Delusional disorder versus schizophreniform and brief psychotic disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 46 year old electrician brought in by his wife. For eight months he has been certain she is having an affair with a neighbour, and he checks her phone, odometer and laundry daily and has begun following her car.

He has continued to run his business without difficulty, meets his contract deadlines and is described by his employees as unchanged in every other respect. He has no hallucinations, his speech is organised, his self care is intact and his mood is not elevated or depressed. His wife confirms the accusations have no basis and that nothing else about him has altered. His urine drug screen is negative and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain is unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Speech organised and goal directed, affect reactive, no hallucinations, no negative symptoms, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; magnetic resonance imaging of the brain unremarkable; full blood count, renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Delusional disorder, jealous type, with function preserved outside the belief itself
options.rationale: A non bizarre delusion of at least one month with no other psychotic symptoms and function not obviously impaired apart from behaviour flowing directly from the belief is the defining pattern (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder, given the eight month duration of psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: Schizophreniform disorder is defined by a duration of one to six months and requires the broader symptom criteria of schizophrenia, neither of which is satisfied at eight months with an isolated delusion (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder, given the abrupt onset of a clearly circumscribed belief
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires full remission within one month, so eight months of continuous symptoms excludes it regardless of how circumscribed the content is (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Paranoid personality disorder with pervasive suspiciousness of his wife and others
options.rationale: Personality disorder requires a pervasive lifelong pattern across relationships, whereas this is a discrete belief that began eight months ago in a man previously described as unchanged (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Obsessive compulsive disorder with poor insight driving his repeated checking rituals
options.rationale: Obsessional checking is driven by doubt and is experienced as unwanted and intrusive, whereas he holds the belief with full conviction and checks to confirm rather than to relieve anxiety (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is easily missed because functioning outside the delusional system is preserved, so patients present late and usually at the instigation of a family member rather than themselves. The three psychotic disorder diagnoses that turn on duration are worth holding as a set: brief psychotic disorder resolves within one month, schizophreniform disorder runs one to six months, and schizophrenia requires six months of disturbance including one month of active symptoms. Delusional disorder sits outside that sequence, requiring one month or more of delusions without the other criteria for schizophrenia. The jealous subtype carries a specific and serious risk of violence towards the accused partner, so a risk assessment that includes the wife's safety is part of the initial management rather than an afterthought.
key_points: Brief psychotic disorder resolves within one month and schizophreniform runs one to six months
Delusional disorder requires one month or more of delusions without other schizophrenia criteria
Function outside the delusional system is characteristically preserved
The jealous subtype carries a specific risk of violence towards the accused partner
explanation.pearls: In delusional jealousy, ask the partner separately about stalking, threats and access to weapons, because the risk assessment that matters concerns a person who is not your patient and who will not be in the room if you do not ask for it.

sources.label: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 28 year old man brought in by friends with agitation and tremor. He has been using a clear liquid he buys in a small bottle and doses every two to three hours around the clock, including overnight, for the past eight months.

His last dose was three hours ago, taken because he woke with the same symptoms. He is sweating, tremulous and repeatedly tries to get off the trolley. He has already received diazepam 20 mg orally in divided doses over the past hour with no discernible change. His breath has no alcoholic smell, his blood alcohol is not detected, and his blood glucose is 5.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 168/96, RR 24, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, diaphoresis, disoriented to time and place, visual hallucinations of insects
data_table.Investigations: Blood alcohol not detected; blood glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.0-7.7); sodium, potassium and creatinine within normal limits; creatine kinase 340 U/L (30-190)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give oral thiamine and manage him with hourly observation in the short stay unit
options.rationale: Thiamine is appropriate supportive care but oral dosing and ward level observation badly underestimate a withdrawal syndrome that can progress to rhabdomyolysis and death within hours (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Give intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg and repeat once after 30 minutes if required
options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not act on the receptor system driving this withdrawal, so they are adjuncts at most and never the primary agent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Escalate to high dose intravenous diazepam titrated in a monitored critical care area
options.rationale: Gamma hydroxybutyrate withdrawal is benzodiazepine responsive but characteristically requires very large and rapidly escalating doses given intravenously, and the failure of 20 mg orally is the expected pattern rather than evidence against the diagnosis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine; Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).

options.text: Commence an intravenous fluid infusion and reassess his agitation in two hours
options.rationale: Fluids address the rhabdomyolysis risk but leave the withdrawal itself untreated, and a two hour reassessment interval is far too long for a syndrome that deteriorates this quickly (Source: Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).

options.text: Commence a buprenorphine and naloxone film and observe for symptom improvement
options.rationale: Opioid substitution treats opioid withdrawal, which does not produce this degree of hyperthermia, hypertension and delirium and is not suggested by the described use pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

explanation.summary: Gamma hydroxybutyrate has a half life of under an hour, so dependent users must dose every two to three hours around the clock and withdrawal begins within hours rather than days of the last dose. The syndrome resembles severe alcohol withdrawal but is faster in onset, more likely to progress to delirium, and notoriously refractory, with reported total diazepam requirements running into hundreds of milligrams. Barbiturates and, in some centres, baclofen are used as adjuncts when benzodiazepine escalation alone is insufficient. Mortality arises from hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmia and aspiration, so management belongs in a critical care environment from the outset.
key_points: Overnight dosing every two to three hours is the historical signature of dependence
Withdrawal begins within hours of the last dose, not days
Benzodiazepine requirements are large, escalate rapidly and are given intravenously
Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and are adjuncts at most
explanation.pearls: A patient who sets an alarm to dose overnight has a substance with a half life under about two hours, which points at gamma hydroxybutyrate rather than alcohol or benzodiazepines before any test result is available.

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural disturbance in Parkinson disease
stem:
You are the medical registrar on call. A 74 year old man admitted two days ago with a urinary tract infection has become acutely agitated overnight. He is pulling at his intravenous line, has struck out at a nurse and cannot be redirected by verbal reassurance or by his wife.

He has Parkinson disease treated with levodopa and carbidopa, and his mobility depends on it. He is disoriented to place and time, and his attention fluctuates markedly over minutes. Reorientation, dimmed lighting and the removal of unnecessary lines have already been tried without effect, and he now poses an immediate risk to himself and to staff. His oxygen saturation, blood glucose, sodium and calcium are within normal limits and he is not in urinary retention.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 142/84, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Examination: Fluctuating attention, disoriented, resting tremor and rigidity, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Sodium, potassium, calcium, blood glucose and liver function within normal limits; bladder scan 40 mL

lead_in: Which medication is the most appropriate choice for immediate sedation?

options.text: Haloperidol 0.5 mg intramuscularly, repeated once after 30 minutes if required
options.rationale: Haloperidol is the usual first choice in hyperactive delirium but its potent dopamine blockade can precipitate a severe and prolonged deterioration in parkinsonian motor function (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Olanzapine 5 mg intramuscularly, repeated once after 30 minutes if required
options.rationale: Olanzapine has less extrapyramidal liability than haloperidol but still worsens motor function in Parkinson disease and is not one of the two agents considered safe in this population (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Risperidone 0.5 mg orally, repeated once after 30 minutes if he remains agitated
options.rationale: Risperidone has the highest extrapyramidal liability of the second generation agents at any effective dose, which makes it a poor choice when nigrostriatal dopamine is already depleted (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg orally, repeated once after 30 minutes if he remains agitated
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines prolong and deepen delirium in older patients and are reserved for alcohol or sedative withdrawal or for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Quetiapine 25 mg orally, repeated once after 30 minutes if he remains agitated
options.rationale: Quetiapine and clozapine are the only antipsychotics with sufficiently loose striatal dopamine binding to be used in Parkinson disease, and quetiapine is the practical choice since clozapine requires haematological monitoring and titration (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Delirium is managed first by treating the precipitant and by non pharmacological measures, and medication is reserved for distress or risk that persists after those have failed, as described here. The default agent in hyperactive delirium is low dose haloperidol, but Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies invert that default because dopamine blockade can produce catastrophic and long lasting motor deterioration or neuroleptic sensitivity reactions. Quetiapine and clozapine dissociate rapidly from the striatal dopamine receptor and are the accepted exceptions. Withdrawing or reducing levodopa to control the agitation is a common error that trades confusion for immobility and risks a parkinsonism hyperpyrexia syndrome.
key_points: Treat the precipitant and use non pharmacological measures before any sedating medication
Haloperidol is the usual first choice in hyperactive delirium but not in Parkinson disease
Quetiapine and clozapine are the antipsychotics tolerated in parkinsonian patients
Benzodiazepines deepen delirium except in withdrawal states or neuroleptic malignant syndrome
explanation.pearls: Never abruptly stop levodopa to settle agitation in Parkinson disease, because withdrawal can precipitate a parkinsonism hyperpyrexia syndrome that is clinically indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
